title: Bartholomew's Wild Ride
markdown:
Bartholomew Buttercup was a mole with apple-rosy cheeks and a twinkle that suggested either a grand secret or a particularly shiny pebble. His greatest joy, besides an earthworm sandwich, was building boats. Not ordinary boats. Bartholomew built boats from theories so thoroughly Bartholomew that other people’s whiskers twitched in self-defence.

His workshop sat beside a gurgling stream, a cheerful lopsided shed where planks escaped, ropes knotted themselves for sport, and tools hummed as if they had hobbies. Here he explained his latest marvel to Pip the badger, who sat on a mossy bank with the patient frown he reserved for theories about to take flight.

“This,” Bartholomew declared, paws conducting an invisible orchestra, “is the dawn of a new era in moving on water. Observe the foundational principles of Aero-Buoyancy.”

Pip blinked. On a wobbly stand sat a bathtub with ambitions. Large, flapping sails hung from poles that looked ready to emigrate.

“The air, that most uncooperative of elements, can be persuaded to lift,” Bartholomew went on. “When the wind rushes over these air-catching parts—” He patted a sail. The sail patted back, showering Pip’s neat fur with sawdust. “—it creates an upward pressure.”

Pip brushed himself down. “It looks very energetic, Bartholomew.”

Bartholomew believed his outlandish theories the way other moles believed in tunnels: completely, and with both paws. Sometimes, because he believed so hard, the world nearly agreed.

“Energetic is the word. Not just buoyant. Aerodynamically buoyant. This Saturday, at the Water Lily Festival, the canal will see a boat that does not merely float. It dances.” He clasped his paws, already hearing applause that had not yet been invented.

Saturday arrived under a blue so cheerful it ought to have been charged rent. A breeze whispered secrets through the reeds, the innocent sort of breeze that has not yet read the afternoon’s script. The canal, usually a calm ribbon, became a hive of ribbons and flower-boats. Owners bustled with pre-race excitement. Oars splashed. Happy chatter hummed. Fruit pies sent their scent across the water from stalls that had taken the festival seriously. Otters, voles, hedgehogs, and a few curious ducks lined the banks, a colourful mosaic of expectation. In the middle of the fuss, the Aero-Buoyancy Vessel waited at the launch point, a monument to mole ambition and questionable physics.

As Bartholomew fussed over a sail that was trying to leave without him, a grumpy old goose waddled up. This was Beca, whose primary occupation was grumbling.

“Buttercup,” Beca honked, rusty as a gate, “that contraption will blow away before it gets wet. A boat needs to float, not flap like a startled pigeon.”

Bartholomew chuckled and adjusted his goggles. “You underestimate applied theory. This is ingenuity with a bathtub attached.”

He climbed in. The crowd leaned. Pip stood ready with a quiet word, which was his version of a life ring.

Then the cheerful sky held its breath and turned a bruised purple. The whisper in the reeds became a howl. Fat rain found Pip’s nose.

“A minor weather hiccup,” Bartholomew called, his voice a little thinner. “A perfect test of stability under duress.”

The wind had other ideas. It whipped the sails into a frenzy. The vessel, designed to glide, bucked and dipped like a duckling tossed in a washtub. Rain drew a silver curtain over worried faces on the bank. A gust flattened Pip against the mud, his usual calm pierced by the thought that Bartholomew was going to be soaked through. He watched, heart thumping like a drum, as the dancing boat was thoroughly, unequivocally battered. It was not dancing. It was being reviewed by weather, and the weather was not kind.

Then the unexpected arrived, as it often did when Bartholomew was involved. Instead of capsizing with dignity or sinking with a disappointed gurgle, the Aero-Buoyancy Vessel caught a combination of tempest and wave and began an aerial ballet nobody had rehearsed. It pirouetted and spun. It dipped and swooped. For brief, thrilling instants it lifted above the chop and hung there like a very surprised, oversized kite that had lost its string and discovered a mischievous spirit.

The rain softened, as if it had seen enough theatre. The wind eased, tired of its own drama. Bartholomew, soaked and miraculously upright, bobbed in the centre of the canal, still clinging, goggles dripping, boat somehow intact.

The crowd came out from awnings. Astonishment warmed into laughter that travelled the water like good news. Even Beca, grumbles mislaid, let out a honk that had decided to be a cheer.

Bartholomew looked around. Aero-Buoyancy had not worked as planned. Not in the slightest. What it had done was give the festival the most exciting, chaotic show anyone could remember. A playful wave tickled his nose. He managed a sheepish grin.

Pip made his way back along the bank, damp and delighted. Bartholomew waved him over, cheeks still rosy under the drenching.

“Well, Bartholomew,” Pip said. “Your theory was certainly lively.”

Bartholomew’s chuckle came up from somewhere earthy and glad. “Sometimes, my dear Pip, the most wonderful theories are the ones that go spectacularly wrong.”

The sun shouldered through the last clouds and laid gold on the calmed canal. The bathtub-boat, accidental marvel, sat as proudly as a vessel that had meant every spin. Bartholomew patted a dripping sail. Pip, on the bank, looked exactly as he had in the workshop — loyal, amused, a little sawdusted by friendship — except now the whole festival had seen what Pip already knew: that a mole’s wild ride could end, not in disaster, but in laughter, and a stream that had remembered how to gurgle.
characters: Bartholomew Buttercup (a cheerful mole boat builder), Pip (a badger friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
